title: Acids, alkalis and titrations
learningObjective: Describe the use of litmus, phenolphthalein and methyl orange to distinguish between acidic and alkaline solutions; Understand how the pH scale, from 0–14, can be used to classify solutions as strongly acidic (0-3), weakly acidic (4–6), neutral (7), weakly alkaline (8–10) and strongly alkaline (11–14); Describe the use of universal indicator to measure the approximate pH value of an aqueous solution; Know that acids in aqueous solution are a source of hydrogen ions and alkalis in a aqueous solution are a source of hydroxide ions; Know that alkalis can neutralise acids; Describe how to carry out an acid-alkali titration

sections.title: Acids, Alkalis and Titrations
sections.markdown:
Some acids you will never touch without full protective clothing and a spill
plan; others you eat by the slice. The citric acid in an orange and the acid
that demands gloves and goggles belong to the same chemical family — what
changes is how much hydrogen ion they release and how concentrated the
solution is. Alkalis have the same spread: the sodium hydroxide that clears
blocked drains and the mild carbonate solutions in household products all sit
on the same scale. This chapter gives you that scale, the tools to tell acids
from alkalis in seconds, and the classic technique chemists use to make them
react in exactly measured amounts: the [[titration]].

Three questions organise the chapter. First, **how do you tell an acid from an alkali?** With [[indicator]]s — the colour-switching dyes [[litmus]],
[[phenolphthalein]] and [[methyl-orange]], and the full-range
[[universal-indicator]] that estimates a pH value. Second, **how acidic or
alkaline is it, exactly?** With the pH scale, which you will learn to read
into five bands from strongly acidic to strongly alkaline. Third, **what is
really happening when they react?** Acids are sources of hydrogen ions,
alkalis are sources of hydroxide ions, and neutralisation is those two ions
meeting to make water — one ionic equation that covers every acid–alkali
reaction you will ever write at this level.

The chapter closes with a skill that belongs to chemistry alone in your
specification: carrying out an acid–alkali titration with burette precision.
Everything you learn here feeds forward — the reactions of acids continue in
Chapter 17 (u2:c17) with salt preparations, and the calculation side of
titrations is waiting in Chapter 6 (u1:c06).

:::prior-knowledge
Three earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 3 (u1:c03) you need the
idea of ions and of ionic compounds existing as separated ions in solution —
spectator-ion reasoning later in the chapter depends on it. From Chapter 5
(u1:c05) you need formulae, balancing and state symbols, because every
equation in this chapter is written in full ionic dress. From Chapter 6
(u1:c06) you will borrow the concentration toolset when titration volumes
turn into calculations. Nothing here needs new maths beyond subtraction to
two decimal places.
:::

:::exam-hint
Five of this chapter's six objectives are examined in both papers — Paper 1C
and Paper 2C. The sixth, describing how to carry out an acid–alkali
titration, is chemistry-only: it appears in Paper 2C only. The recurring
question shapes are: state the colours an indicator shows in acidic and
alkaline solutions; classify solutions into the five pH bands; write
equations for acid + base and acid + alkali, then the ionic equation; and
describe the titration method step by step. Watch the command words:
*state* wants a colour or a number, *describe* wants the method in order,
*explain* wants the ions.
:::

:::misconception
"An indicator tells you the pH of a solution." Not the three you must name
for the exam. Litmus, phenolphthalein and methyl orange each show just two
colours — they can only sort a solution into acidic or alkaline. Only
universal indicator, which blends several dyes, gives an approximate pH
value by the colour it turns. Choosing the right indicator for the job is
itself an exam skill this chapter teaches.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.28 orientation items. Before moving on, name the
three single-colour-change indicators you must know, and say in one sentence
what kind of information each one can and cannot give you. If you can also
say which objective of this chapter is chemistry-only, the route map is
fixed in your head.
:::

sections.title: Ph and Indicators
sections.markdown:
The [[ph-scale]] runs from about 0 to about 14, and each number is a verdict
on a solution: how acidic or how alkaline it is. The scale pivots on 7. Below
7 the solution is acidic, and the further below, the more acidic; above 7 it
is alkaline, and the further above, the more alkaline; exactly 7 is neutral.
Vinegar, for example — a solution of ethanoic acid — sits a few units below
7, while drain-clearing sodium hydroxide sits near the top.

The scale is not just a number line: the specification wants you to sort
solutions into five named bands. Learn the boundaries and an everyday example
of each, because classification questions ask for the band by name.

| Classification | pH | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|
| [[strongly-acidic]] | 0–3 | hydrochloric acid |
| [[weakly-acidic]] | 4–6 | ethanoic acid (vinegar) |
| neutral | 7 | sodium chloride (solution) |
| [[weakly-alkaline]] | 8–10 | ammonia (solution) |
| [[strongly-alkaline]] | 11–14 | sodium hydroxide |

Two conventions earn easy marks. When you write pH, it is a small p and a
capital H — the H is the symbol for hydrogen, and by the end of this chapter
you will see exactly why the symbol belongs there. And when a question gives
you a pH value, answer with the band word ("weakly acidic"), not just
"acidic": the band is the classification, and the mark scheme wants it.

[[litmus]] is the indicator attached to this band system. It works either as
a solution or soaked into litmus paper, and it sorts any solution for you:
red in acid, blue in alkali.

:::key-point
Litmus can be used as a solution or as litmus paper — either form gives the
same red-in-acid, blue-in-alkali verdict. When writing pH, it is a small p
and a big H (the symbol for hydrogen).
:::

:::exam-hint
A pH meter measures pH far more accurately than any indicator — in method
questions, naming a pH meter (with its digital readout) is the accurate
instrument, while universal indicator is the approximate one. And treat the
five bands as approximate boundaries, not walls: the edges depend on
concentration, so a 0.10 mol/dm³ solution of ethanoic acid already measures
pH 2.88 — inside the strongly acidic band even though it is a modest
concentration of a weak acid.
:::

:::misconception
"'Strongly acidic' means a high concentration of acid has been dissolved."
The band describes the pH of the solution, not the amount of acid dissolved
in it. A modest 0.10 mol/dm³ solution of ethanoic acid sits at pH 2.88,
deep in the strongly acidic band, because pH tracks the hydrogen ions in
solution — not the mass of acid you started with. Concentration and pH are
related, but they are not the same measurement.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.29 classification items. Classify each by band:
hydrochloric acid, vinegar, sodium chloride solution, ammonia solution,
sodium hydroxide solution. Then write the symbol correctly from memory —
small p, capital H. If all five bands came out right, you are ready to
measure.
:::

sections.title: Measuring Ph
sections.markdown:
Litmus answers one question — acid or alkali. To measure the pH itself you
need an indicator whose colour slides through a range, and that is
[[universal-indicator]]: a mixture of indicators blended so their colours
merge into a gradual sweep across the whole [[ph-scale]]. Full-range
universal indicator changes through a ladder of colours from pH 1 to pH 14,
as a solution or as paper. You compare the colour against a chart and read
off the approximate pH. The word approximate matters — this is an estimate,
not a precise measurement.

The blending idea behind it generalises: any substance whose colour depends
on pH can serve as an [[indicator]]. Four matter for your exam, and you must
know their colours in acidic and in alkaline solutions without hesitation.

| Indicator | In acid | In alkali |
|---|---|---|
| [[litmus]] | red | blue |
| [[methyl-orange]] | red | yellow |
| [[phenolphthalein]] | colourless | pink |
| universal indicator | red | blue |

Neutral solutions complete the picture. Litmus is purple in a neutral
solution — not a third dye but an equal mixture of its red and blue forms,
which is exactly why it sits at the halfway point of its own colour story.
Universal indicator reads green at pH 7. While you are here, fix the five
formulae you will use all year: hydrochloric acid HCl, nitric acid HNO₃,
sulfuric acid H₂SO₄, ethanoic acid CH₃COOH and phosphoric acid H₃PO₄ — the
[[acid]]s whose replaceable hydrogens power the next section.

:::exam-hint
Colour-memory questions are free marks if you file the pairs, not the
list: litmus red/blue, methyl orange red/yellow, phenolphthalein
colourless/pink, universal indicator red/blue. Phenolphthalein is the one
that starts colourless — that makes it the indicator of choice for titration
endpoints, where a colour *appearing* is easier to see than one vanishing
— the titration section of this chapter shows you why. Universal indicator is the only one
that estimates a pH value; the other three only sort acidic from alkaline.
:::

:::misconception
"Universal indicator is the most accurate indicator, so always choose it."
Its gradual, many-coloured sweep is precisely its weakness: it gives an
approximate pH, it is not very accurate compared with a pH meter, and its
slow blend of colours makes it useless for detecting a sharp endpoint in a
titration. Accuracy belongs to the pH meter; sharpness belongs to the
single-colour-change indicators; universality belongs to universal
indicator. Each tool has its own job.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.28 and 2.30 items. From memory, fill a four-row
table: each indicator against its acid colour and its alkali colour. Then
add the two neutral colours — litmus and universal indicator. Finally, state
which single indicator could tell you whether a solution is closer to pH 3
or pH 5, and why the other three cannot.
:::

*Extension.* At the next level of study, pH stops being a scale you memorise
and becomes a quantity you compute: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺(aq)], the negative
logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration. That equation explains a
curiosity you will meet at the end of this chapter — why one drop of alkali
near an endpoint can leap the reading from about pH 3 to about pH 11.

sections.title: Acids
sections.markdown:
Every [[acid]] has one structural signature: its molecules contain hydrogen,
and when the acid reacts it is that hydrogen which takes part — the
[[replaceable-hydrogen]]. In the catalogue you met in the previous section,
the replaceable hydrogens are the ones that can be swapped for something
else. React hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide and the swap is visible
in the equation:

HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

The H of the HCl has been replaced by an Na, and water is what the displaced
hydrogen becomes. Sulfuric acid carries two replaceable hydrogens and
phosphoric acid three; hydrochloric and nitric acid carry one each.

But not every hydrogen in a formula is replaceable. Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH,
holds four hydrogens — yet only the one attached to the oxygen ever reacts.
The three bolted to the carbon never budge. (Where that O-attached hydrogen
family leads is Chapter 27's story: u4:c27, carboxylic acids.)

What acids do in water is the definition that earns the marks. In aqueous
solution an [[acid]] dissociates — it breaks apart — releasing [[hydrogen-ion]]s:

HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)

This is why measuring pH is really measuring ions: when you measure the pH
of a solution you are measuring the concentration of H⁺ ions in it. It is
also why the H in pH is a capital H — the symbol is literally the hydrogen
it measures. And it gives the definition the mark scheme wants: acids are
substances that act as a source of hydrogen ions (H⁺) in solution.

:::exam-hint
The one-line acid definition is a reliable mark: "a source of hydrogen ions
(H⁺) in solution". Keep the H⁺ in brackets and keep the word *source* —
"acids contain hydrogen" is true but scores nothing, because the marks are
for the ions the acid releases in water. If a question asks why pH carries
a capital H, the answer runs through this same idea: pH measures the
hydrogen ion concentration.
:::

:::misconception
"Every hydrogen in an acid's formula takes part in its reactions." Only the
replaceable hydrogens do. In ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, three of the four
hydrogens are attached to carbon and never react — only the hydrogen on the
oxygen is replaceable. Counting hydrogens in a formula and counting
reactive hydrogens are different skills, and confusing them loses marks in
both directions.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.31 acids-half items. Say the acid definition in
one sentence with the ion in brackets; write the equation for HCl
dissociating in water; and state which of the four hydrogens in CH₃COOH is
replaceable. Those three answers are the acid half of this chapter's ion
story.
:::

sections.title: Bases
sections.markdown:
A [[base]] is the mirror of an [[acid]]: bases neutralise acids by combining
with the hydrogen ions in them. At this level, a base means a metal oxide, a
metal hydroxide, or ammonia (NH₃). Copper(II) oxide and magnesium oxide are
bases you will react with acids this year; the black powder disappearing into
hot dilute sulfuric acid to give a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate is the
picture to keep.

Some bases go one step further: they dissolve in water to form solutions
containing [[hydroxide-ion]]s. These soluble bases are [[alkali]]s, and they
complete the ion story of this chapter — as acids are a source of hydrogen
ions, so alkalis are a source of hydroxide (OH⁻) ions in solution. The Group
1 hydroxides are the everyday examples: sodium hydroxide and potassium
hydroxide. In water, sodium hydroxide dissociates completely:

NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

Ammonia is the alkali that behaves differently — it does not contain a
hydroxide to release. Instead, the dissolved ammonia reacts with the water to
make ammonium ions and hydroxide ions:

NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) → NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

You will meet this solution labelled "ammonium hydroxide" on cleaning-product
bottles; add universal indicator and it shows the blue-green of an alkali.
Every alkali in this family — hydroxides and ammonia solution alike — has a
pH greater than 7.

There are other routes to alkaline solutions too. Soluble metal carbonates
react with water to release hydroxide ions; the ionic equation at the next
level is CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) → OH⁻(aq) + HCO₃⁻(aq). The next section takes
one of those carbonate alkalis as its whole subject.

:::exam-hint
Keep the two definitions strictly paired: acid = source of H⁺(aq); alkali =
source of OH⁻(aq). The examiner's favourite follow-up is the relationship
between base and alkali — all alkalis are bases, but only bases that
dissolve in water producing hydroxide ions are alkalis. Copper(II) oxide is
the standard counter-example: a base, but insoluble, so not an alkali.
:::

:::misconception
"'Base' and 'alkali' are two words for the same thing." They overlap but are
not identical. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give hydroxide
ions; a base is anything that neutralises an acid by combining with its
hydrogen ions — including insoluble oxides such as copper(II) oxide and
magnesium oxide. Calling copper(II) oxide an alkali is a genuine chemistry
error, not a wording quibble.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.31 alkalis-half and 2.32 items. Write the two
dissociation equations (sodium hydroxide; ammonia with water), then explain
in one sentence why copper(II) oxide is a base but not an alkali. If the
phrase "source of hydroxide ions" is in your second sentence, the alkali
half of the story is yours.
:::

sections.title: Reacting Acids with Alkalis
sections.markdown:
Very few carbonates dissolve in water — but two of the exceptions are
chemicals you will handle constantly. Sodium carbonate and potassium
carbonate both dissolve to give [[alkali]] solutions with a pH greater than
7. Where does the alkalinity come from? Not from any hydroxide in their
formula — Na₂CO₃ and K₂CO₃ contain carbonate, not hydroxide. The alkalinity
is the hydrolysis you met in the previous section: the dissolved carbonate
ions react with water and release [[hydroxide-ion]]s.

What makes these solutions only [[weakly-alkaline]] is a matter of supply.
Only some of the carbonate ions react with water at any moment, so the
hydroxide concentration stays modest — the solution climbs above pH 7 into
the weakly alkaline band (8–10), but never approaches the strength of sodium
hydroxide, which dissociates completely. It is a neat piece of evidence for
the band system: two alkalis, both above pH 7, occupying different bands for
a reason you can now state.

:::exam-hint
"Explain why sodium carbonate solution is only weakly alkaline" has a
two-step answer shape: carbonate ions react with water to produce hydroxide
ions (that is the alkalinity), but only partially — so the OH⁻
concentration stays low and the pH sits in the weakly alkaline band rather
than the strongly alkaline one. Naming the band earns the classification
mark; the partial-reaction explanation earns the chemistry mark.
:::

:::misconception
"All carbonates are alkalis." Solubility decides, and most metal carbonates
are insoluble — copper(II) carbonate will never form an alkaline solution
because it will not dissolve. Only the soluble ones, sodium and potassium
carbonate among them, can release hydroxide ions into water and count as
alkalis. The word "soluble" is doing real work in every carbonate
definition.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.31/2.32 carbonate items. Name the two soluble
carbonate alkalis, and explain in two steps why their solutions are only
weakly alkaline. If your second step says "only some of the carbonate ions
react with water", you have the examiner's sentence.
:::

sections.title: Reacting Acids with Bases and Alkalis
sections.markdown:
When an [[acid]] meets a [[base]] or an [[alkali]], the reaction has a name:
[[neutralisation]]. The acid's hydrogen ions are consumed, and the products
tell the story — a salt and water. Two worked examples carry the whole idea,
one for each kind of reactant.

**Acid + base.** Copper(II) oxide is a metal oxide — a base. React it with
hot dilute sulfuric acid and the black powder dissolves to a blue solution:

CuO(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CuSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)

Copper(II) oxide is an ionic compound built from Cu²⁺ and O²⁻ ions, so the
mechanism is pure ion chemistry: the H⁺ ions from the acid combine with the
O²⁻ ions from the base to form water, and the copper and sulfate ions are
left holding the solution together as copper(II) sulfate.

**Acid + alkali.** Sodium hydroxide solution reacts with dilute hydrochloric
acid to give sodium chloride and water:

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

Both sodium hydroxide and sodium chloride are ionic, so in solution every
one of them exists as separated ions — and HCl, being an acid, dissociates
into H⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq). Rewrite the equation with every ion shown and
something jumps out: the Na⁺(aq) and Cl⁻(aq) appear identically on both
sides. They are [[spectator-ion]]s — present, but unchanged. Strike them
out and what remains is the reaction itself, written as an
[[ionic-equation]]:

H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)

This single line is the deepest idea in the chapter: every neutralisation
between an acid and an alkali has this same ionic equation, because every
one of them is the same event — the alkali's OH⁻ ions and the acid's H⁺
ions joining to make water. Change the acid, change the alkali, change the
salt; the reaction never changes.

:::exam-hint
Equation questions in this topic come in a reliable order: full formula
equation first, then identify the spectator ions, then the ionic equation.
State the spectators by name ("Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are unchanged on both sides")
before you cancel them — the cancellation is worth marks only once it is
justified. And "write the ionic equation for the reaction between any acid
and any alkali" is a gift question: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), every time.
:::

:::misconception
"Neutralisation needs an alkali, and alkalis are the only things that
neutralise acids." The copper(II) oxide example says otherwise: it is a
base, not an alkali — insoluble in water — yet it neutralises sulfuric acid
completely. What neutralisation requires is something that combines with
hydrogen ions: oxides, hydroxides and alkalis all qualify. Alkalis are a
sub-family of neutralisers, not the only one.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.32 neutralisation items. Write the balanced full
equation for magnesium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid. Then, for the
sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid reaction, name the spectator ions and
write the ionic equation. Finish in reverse: which two ions appear in the
ionic equation of *every* acid–alkali neutralisation?
:::

sections.title: Titration
sections.markdown:
A [[neutralisation]] on paper is over in one line of equation; in the lab
you want to know exactly *how much* acid reacts with exactly how much alkali.
The [[titration]] is how you find out. One solution of known volume sits in
a conical flask with a few drops of indicator; the other runs in from a
[[burette]] until the indicator flips colour — and the burette reading tells
you the reacting volume to a fiftieth of a cubic centimetre. (What you do
with those volumes — the concentration calculations — is Chapter 6's
toolkit: u1:c06.)

The method has a rhythm, and the description of it is itself examinable —
this is the one objective in the chapter assessed in Paper 2C only:

1. **Rough run first.** Add alkali from the burette to the acid until the
   indicator changes colour, reading roughly. If the rough run needed about
   22.50 cm³, that number is your map for the accurate runs.
2. **Accurate run, fast then slow.** Repeat with a fresh mixture. Run in
   about 20 cm³ quite quickly, swirling the conical flask constantly to mix
   the solutions — then slow to a drip.
3. **Dropwise to the flip.** Add the alkali one drop at a time until a
   single drop changes the indicator from its acid colour to its alkali
   colour. You now know the neutralisation volume to within one drop — as
   precise as the technique allows.
4. **Choose the direction deliberately.** You could run acid into alkali
   instead, but with phenolphthalein the alkali-into-acid direction wins:
   watching colourless turn pink is easier on the eye than watching pink
   vanish.

Phenolphthalein is the classic choice because of exactly that sharp,
two-colour flip. [[methyl-orange]] works too. What must never be used is
[[universal-indicator]]: its colours change gradually through a whole range,
so there is no single unmistakable moment to call the endpoint.

Reading the burette has its own law. The scale runs the opposite way to
every measuring cylinder you have used: 0 sits at the top and 50 at the
bottom, so the numbers grow as the liquid level falls. Record every reading to two decimal places — the nearest
0.05 cm³. The second decimal place is a 0 when the meniscus sits on a scale
line and a 5 when it sits between two lines. Subtract initial from final and
you have the volume delivered.

:::key-point
The [[endpoint]] is the point at which the indicator changes colour — and it
does not necessarily coincide with the point where the solution is exactly
neutral. Near the endpoint the pH changes extremely fast: in some titrations
a single drop of alkali swings the pH from about 3 to about 11. That is why
knowing the neutralisation point to within one drop is the precision ceiling
of the technique.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Describe how to carry out an acid–alkali titration" — six beats, in order:
measure the fixed volume with a pipette into a conical flask; add a few
drops of indicator; fill the burette with the other solution and note the
initial reading (two decimal places); run it in fast-then-dropwise with
swirling; stop at the first permanent colour change; record the final
reading and subtract. Practise questions hand you results tables — final
reading minus initial reading gives the volume delivered, and the table
usually shows the two-decimal law already applied.
:::

:::misconception
"The endpoint of a titration is the moment the solution becomes neutral."
Close, and wrong. The endpoint is defined by the *indicator's* colour
change; the neutral point is defined by the chemistry. They are close enough
for excellent results precisely because the pH leaps so steeply near
neutralisation — but they are not the same event, and the one-drop pH swing
from about 3 to about 11 is the evidence.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.33C technique items. Answer without looking: why
are burette readings recorded to two decimal places, and what does the
second decimal place depend on? Why is universal indicator never used in a
titration? What is the endpoint, and why is it not exactly the neutral
point?
:::

sections.title: End of Chemistry Only
sections.markdown:
This section closes the chapter — and with it, the chemistry-only ribbon
that has run through the last stretch of Unit 2. Everything the chapter
taught now compresses into six abilities, one per objective, and each one is
a question shape you will meet on the page.

:::summary
The pH scale runs from about 0 to about 14 and sorts solutions into five
bands: strongly acidic (0–3), weakly acidic (4–6), neutral (7), weakly
alkaline (8–10) and strongly alkaline (11–14). Indicators read that
chemistry for you: litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein each give one
acid colour and one alkali colour, while universal indicator sweeps the
whole scale and estimates an approximate pH against a chart. Beneath the
colours, acids are sources of hydrogen ions and alkalis are sources of
hydroxide ions — sodium hydroxide dissociates straight to Na⁺ + OH⁻, ammonia
makes its OH⁻ by reacting with water, and soluble carbonates top up OH⁻
partially, which is why they are only weakly alkaline. Neutralisation is
those two ions meeting: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), the one ionic equation
behind every acid–alkali reaction, with the spectators struck out. And the
[[titration]] turns that chemistry into a measured volume: rough run, fast
then dropwise, one drop to the [[endpoint]], burette readings to two
decimal places.
:::

:::can-you
Keyed to the six objectives, in order: state the colours of litmus, methyl
orange and phenolphthalein in acidic and in alkaline solutions (2.28);
classify any given pH into its band and name an everyday example of each
band (2.29); describe universal indicator and say why its pH reading is
only approximate (2.30); define acid and alkali by their ions, with the
equations for NaOH and NH₃ in water (2.31); explain neutralisation with the
ionic equation and identify the spectator ions in a full equation (2.32);
and describe the full titration method — pipette, indicator, burette,
swirling, dropwise, two-decimal readings (2.33C, Paper 2C only).
:::

:::exam-hint
The chemistry-only flag matters for revision planning: the titration
objective is assessed in Paper 2C only, so Paper 1 never asks you to
describe the method — but the other five objectives of this chapter are
examined in both papers. Practice for all six objectives joins from the
platform question bank by spec ref, and the titration calculations
themselves wait in Chapter 6 (u1:c06).
:::

:::misconception
"'Chemistry only' means harder, so everyone should revise it first." It
means no such thing about difficulty — it means the Science Double Award
route never examines 2.33C, so Chemistry candidates meet titration
technique as their exclusive territory. The five shared objectives carry
the marks in both papers; the chemistry-only objective adds the technique
marks on top in Paper 2C.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Titration is one of chemistry's great exports. Pharmaceutical labs titrate
to verify the strength of every batch of medicine before it ships; the food
and drink industry checks acidity the same way — the citric acid of this
chapter's opening oranges is graded by titration in juice production;
environmental agencies run acid-rain monitoring by titrating rainfall
samples. The burette skills you are building are the same ones Quality
Control chemists clock in with — and the pH-band vocabulary of this chapter
is the language their reports are written in.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.28–2.33C close-out items. Run the six-ability
self-test in the can-you list above cold, in order, and flag any ability
you cannot state in one sentence — that flag is your revision list for
this chapter.
:::
